title: Erdos #103 OQ-01: Does h(n) tend to infinity?
description: Investigation of whether h(n), the count of incongruent optimal point configurations with minimum separation 1 and minimal diameter, tends to infinity. Proves isometry injectivity, constructs isometry inverses, eliminates congruent_symm sorry, and demonstrates that the parent file's 'unbounded iff tends to infinity' equivalence is logically false without monotonicity.

meta.historicalContext: Erdos Problem #103 (1994) asks whether h(n) -> infinity, where h(n) counts incongruent sets of n points in R^2 minimizing diameter with separation >= 1. Even h(n) >= 2 for all large n is unknown. This investigation reveals a subtle logical error in the original formalization: the claim that 'h unbounded' is equivalent to 'h -> infinity' requires monotonicity, which is itself an open structural question.

overview.historicalContext: Erdős Problem #103, first appearing in his 1994 collection "Some of my favourite unsolved problems," asks whether h(n) → ∞, where h(n) counts the number of incongruent sets of n points in ℝ² that minimize diameter subject to pairwise distances ≥ 1. The problem connects to the classical theory of optimal point configurations studied by Fejes Tóth (1953) and to modern questions about the structure of extremal packings. The parent formalization contained a subtle logical error: it claimed that "h unbounded" and "h tends to infinity" are equivalent, but this requires monotonicity of h, which is itself an interesting open structural question about how the space of optimal configurations evolves as the number of points increases.
overview.problemStatement:
**Investigation**: Does h(n) -> infinity as n -> infinity, where h(n) counts incongruent sets of n points in R^2 that minimize diameter subject to d(x,y) >= 1?

**Key finding**: The 'unbounded <=> tends to infinity' equivalence claimed in the parent formalization is FALSE without monotonicity. We prove the correct version and demonstrate the failure with a concrete counterexample.
overview.text: Investigation of whether h(n), the count of incongruent optimal point configurations, tends to infinity. Corrects a logical error in the parent formalization.
overview.proofStrategy: 1. Build pointDist metric properties (definiteness, symmetry) from scratch. 2. Prove isometry injectivity from metric definiteness. 3. Axiomatize surjectivity (Mazur-Ulam), construct inverse. 4. Prove congruent_symm (eliminates parent sorry). 5. Construct oscillating counterexample showing unbounded != tends to infinity. 6. State correct equivalence with monotonicity.
keyInsights: **Metric definiteness enables injectivity**: d(sigma(p), sigma(q)) = 0 => d(p,q) = 0 => p = q. This is the bridge from distance preservation to injectivity.

**Surjective inverse construction**: Given injectivity (proved) and surjectivity (axiom), Function.surjInv gives a genuine two-sided inverse. The key insight is that sigma^{-1}(sigma(p)) = p follows from injectivity applied to sigma(sigma^{-1}(sigma(p))) = sigma(p).

**Counterexample to equivalence**: The function n -> n (if even), 0 (if odd) is unbounded (spikes to 2(C+1) for any C) but does NOT tend to infinity (every odd number gives value 0). This shows the parent file's conjecture_equiv backward direction is logically impossible.
**Monotonicity is the missing hypothesis**: For monotone f, f(N) > C and n >= N imply f(n) >= f(N) > C. Without monotonicity, large values on a subsequence don't propagate to all subsequent terms.

**Monotonicity of h is an open structural question**: Whether adding one more point can only increase the diversity of optimal configurations is plausible (boundary effects) but unproven. This connects to deep questions about the geometry of optimal packings.
prerequisites: Real analysis: metric space properties, square root

sections.title: Problem Overview and Imports
sections.summary: Documents Erdős Problem #103 and the investigation goals: metric properties, isometry group structure, counterexample to unbounded↔tends-to-infinity, and corrected conjecture formulation. Imports Mathlib.

sections.title: Core Definitions
sections.summary: Defines PointConfig, pointDist (Euclidean distance), HasMinSeparation, Isometry2D (distance-preserving map), and AreCongruent (related by isometry).
sections.mathContext: A point configuration is $\text{Fin}\, n \to \mathbb{R}^2$. Distance $d(p,q) = \sqrt{(p_1-q_1)^2 + (p_2-q_2)^2}$. Configurations $P \cong Q$ if $\exists \sigma$ distance-preserving with $Q_i = \sigma(P_i)$.

sections.title: pointDist Metric Properties
sections.summary: Proves pointDist is nonneg, reflexive (d(p,p)=0), symmetric, and definite (d(p,q)=0 iff p=q). Definiteness uses sq_eq_zero_iff to extract p.1=q.1, p.2=q.2 from squared distance = 0.

sections.title: Isometry Properties and Group Structure
sections.summary: Proves isometry injectivity from definiteness. Axiomatizes surjectivity (Mazur-Ulam). Constructs identity, composition, and inverse isometries. Proves inv_comp (left inverse) and comp_inv (right inverse).
sections.mathContext: Injectivity: $\sigma(p) = \sigma(q) \Rightarrow d(\sigma(p), \sigma(q)) = 0 \Rightarrow d(p,q) = 0 \Rightarrow p = q$. Inverse: $\sigma^{-1} = \text{surjInv}(\sigma)$, a two-sided inverse by injectivity + surjectivity.

sections.title: Congruence Equivalence Relation
sections.summary: Proves congruence is reflexive (via identity isometry), symmetric (via inverse isometry, eliminating sorry from parent), and transitive (via composition). Also proves congruence preserves minimum separation.
sections.mathContext: Symmetry: $P \cong Q$ via $\sigma \Rightarrow Q \cong P$ via $\sigma^{-1}$, since $\sigma^{-1}(Q_i) = \sigma^{-1}(\sigma(P_i)) = P_i$.

sections.title: Unbounded Does Not Imply Tends to Infinity
sections.summary: Defines the oscillating function (n if even, 0 if odd). Proves it is unbounded (take n=2(C+1)) and does NOT tend to infinity (odd 2N+1 always gives 0). Combines these to show the general implication fails.
sections.mathContext: Define $f(n) = n$ if $n$ even, $f(n) = 0$ if $n$ odd. Then $\forall C, \exists n, f(n) > C$ but $\neg(\forall C, \exists N, \forall n \geq N, f(n) > C)$.

sections.title: Correct Equivalence with Monotonicity
sections.summary: Proves: for monotone f, unbounded iff tends to infinity. States corrected conjecture formulation for h(n) requiring monotonicity.
sections.mathContext: For monotone $f$: $f(N_0) > C$ and $n \geq N_0 \Rightarrow f(n) \geq f(N_0) > C$.

sections.title: Conjecture Hierarchy and Structural Questions
sections.summary: Defines the conjecture chain: Strong (h→∞) => Weak (h≥2 eventually) => Very Weak (h≥2 infinitely often). Highlights monotonicity of h as an independent open question.
sections.mathContext: Strong: $\forall C, \exists N, \forall n \geq N, h(n) > C$. Weak: $\exists N, \forall n \geq N, h(n) \geq 2$. Very weak: $\forall N, \exists n \geq N, h(n) \geq 2$.

conclusion.summary: This formalization corrects a logical error in the parent Erdos 103 file and builds proper infrastructure for the congruence relation. 23 theorems proved (0 sorries), 1 new axiom (isometry surjectivity). Key contributions: congruent_symm proof (eliminates parent sorry), counterexample to unbounded<=>tendsto equivalence, correct formulation with monotonicity.
conclusion.implications: The distinction between 'unbounded' and 'tends to infinity' is crucial for the Erdos 103 conjecture. Resolving whether h(n) is monotone would either validate the simpler 'unbounded' formulation or reveal that the conjecture requires the stronger 'tends to infinity' statement. This connects to deep questions about how optimal packing configurations evolve with n.
openQuestions: Is h monotone? Does adding one point to an optimal configuration always allow at least as many incongruent optimal configurations?
Can we compute h(4)? The optimal 4-point configuration with separation >= 1 and minimal diameter is known, but counting incongruent optima requires careful analysis.
Is h eventually monotone (monotone for n >= N0)? This weaker condition still suffices for the equivalence.
Can boundary perturbation arguments provide lower bounds on h(n) for large n?
